newsitem.title: INDIA: India says broadcast regulator to have wide powers.
newsitem.headline: India says broadcast regulator to have wide powers.

text.p: India's broadcast regulator, which will be set up under a planned law to free up the air waves, will have the power to enforce competition, Information and Broadcasting Minister Jaipal Reddy said on Tuesday.
"We will try to create a competitive environment," Reddy told a seminar on the proposed law in the Indian capital.
"The broadcasting authority will have sufficient discretion to vary the conditions of the licence (for broadcast) depending upon the circumstances of each case," he said.

In May, Reddy introduced in parliament a draft of the Broadcast Bill and sent it to a multi-party committee of lawmakers who are examining the bill amid intense lobbying by foreign and domestic broadcasters.
The bill is expected to be put to a vote in parliament later this year after the committee proposes changes.
"We as a government have an open mind. This bill will be no more than a working draft," Reddy said.
The Broadcast Bill will allow private broadcasters to beam radio and television programmes from Indian soil, limited for decades by a state monopoly, over the air waves.
State-run All India Radio (AIR) and Doordarshan television currently rent out time slots to private broadcasters, but private broadcasting stations are not allowed.

The Broadcast Bill has irked foreign firms because it would limit their stakes in satellite broadcast companies to 49 percent and totally bar foreign equity in private firms bidding for terrestrial, or local, broadcasting licences.

The bill would also slap a string of licensing conditions on foreign satellite broadcasters currently beaming freely into Indian homes, and impose severe restrictions on the number of licences a broadcaster can hold.
Key interests that could be affected by the legislation are the Hong Kong-based STAR Television, owned by media baron Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd, and U.S.-based NBC, owned by General Electric Co.
"Since it is a sensitive and complex legislation in a virgin area, I decided to refer it to the joint select committee," Reddy said.

The committee on Tuesday published newspaper advertisements inviting viewpoints on the Broadcast Bill, which encompasses issues ranging from terrestrial, cable and direct-to-home (DTH) satellite broadcasting.

In a separate but related move, the government is preparing to set up Prasar Bharati, uniting All India Radio and Doordarshan in an autonomous corporation fashioned after the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC).

Reddy said the government was taking care to ensure public ownership of Prasar Bharati, as it would control as many as 800 television transmitters and hundreds of radio stations counting for assets worth an estimated 550 billion rupees ($15 billion).
The minister said the parliamentary committee would consider all issues, including the foreign broadcasters' demand that their existing equity stakes be protected.
But Reddy said media could not be treated in the same way as other industries, which have been exposed to competition under a wide-ranging economic reform programme launched in 1991.
"Information products are qualitatively different from any other product," Reddy said. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
